summary: Describes the Leighton-Micali hash-based signature system, which builds on work by Lamport, Diffie, Winternitz, and Merkle. It specifies a one-time signature scheme and a general signature scheme that rely only on hash functions, not large-integer math, and are suitable for compact implementations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way to sign messages using only scrambling functions, like a stamp that can only be used a limited number of times. It is designed to stay safe even against very powerful future computers.

questions: why are hash-based signatures quantum resistant
what is a stateful signature scheme
subtitle: Digital signatures built only from hash functions, designed to stay secure even if quantum computers are built.

tldr.problem: Common signature schemes rely on large-integer mathematics, and hash-based signatures offer an alternative that is compact, simple and would still be secure even if an attacker could build a quantum computer.
tldr.mechanism: LM-OTS signs one message per key using chains of hash iterations. LMS puts many one-time keys at the leaves of a Merkle tree whose root is the public key, and HSS stacks several such trees so a large number of signatures can be made.
tldr.outcome: Signing is stateful: a one-time private key must never be reused, so implementations must save the updated state before releasing a signature or forgeries become possible.

today: RFC 8554 is an Informational document from the IRTF's Crypto Forum Research Group, not an Internet Standards Track specification. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Hash-Based Signatures in Brief
sections.content:
RFC 8554 describes the Leighton-Micali adaptation of earlier one-time and tree-based signature systems by Lamport, Diffie, Winternitz and Merkle. A signature system gives asymmetric authentication: a private key signs a message and a public key verifies the pair. These schemes use only hash functions, not large-integer maths.

The trade-offs are small private and public keys and fast signing and verification, but large signatures and moderately slow key generation compared with RSA and ECDSA. A one-time signature (OTS) system can safely sign one message per key pair; an N-time system can sign N or fewer. The document defines three pieces: LM-OTS (one-time), LMS (a Merkle-tree N-time scheme) and HSS (a hierarchy of LMS trees).

Section 1.1 carries a CFRG warning. The authors are confident in the schemes' security against quantum computers given current knowledge, but the schemes are stateful: the secret key changes over time and, if a secret key state is used twice, no security guarantees remain. Developers should not use them except in systems that prevent reuse of key state, and the API MUST allow the signing algorithm to update the secret key state.
sections.eli5: This is a way to sign things using only scrambling machines called hash functions. It is built to stay safe from very powerful future computers, but you must be careful never to use the same one-time stamp twice.

sections.title: LM-OTS: One-Time Signatures
sections.content:
LM-OTS signs a hash of the message. The private key is p secret n-byte strings. The public key is made by applying the hash H repeatedly to each one, 2^w - 1 times, and hashing all the results together. The parameter w is the width in bits of each digit taken from the message hash and is one of 1, 2, 4 or 8.

To sign, the signer hashes the message together with a random n-byte value C, appends a checksum, and splits the result into w-bit digits. Each digit says how many times to apply H to the matching private value, and the intermediate results form the signature. A verifier finishes each chain and checks that the result matches the public key.

The checksum matters. An attacker can freely advance any hash chain, which would let them move a digit upward. The checksum goes down whenever a digit goes up, so such a forgery would require going backwards along a chain, which the one-way hash prevents.

The value of w is a space and time trade-off: a larger w gives a shorter signature but more hashing. With SHA-256 and n = 32, signatures are 8516, 4292, 2180 and 1124 bytes for w of 1, 2, 4 and 8.
sections.eli5: Think of a long ladder of scrambled values. Your message tells you how many rungs to climb on each ladder, and the checksum makes sure a cheat can only climb up, never back down.

sections.title: LMS: A Tree of One-Time Keys
sections.content:
The Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) method signs a large but fixed number of messages. Each LMS key pair has a perfect binary tree of height h with 2^h leaves. Each leaf holds the public key of one LM-OTS key pair, each interior node is the hash of its two children, and the root is the LMS public key. The defined heights are 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 with SHA-256 and 32-byte nodes.

An LMS signature contains the leaf number q, the LM-OTS signature, a typecode and an authentication path: the sibling node at each level from the leaf up to the root, h values in all. The verifier recomputes the LM-OTS public key, hashes up the tree using the path, and checks that the result equals the root.

The private key tracks the next unused leaf. Before releasing a signature, the signer MUST increment q, and if the key lives in nonvolatile memory it MUST make sure the incremented value has been stored. Otherwise a crash and reboot could cause two signatures from one OTS key, letting an attacker forge a third message.

Every hash input starts with a 16-byte random key identifier I and a node or leaf number, plus a fixed two-byte domain separator (0x8080, 0x8181, 0x8282 or 0x8383) so no two kinds of hash call share an input format.
sections.eli5: Imagine a tree where every leaf is a single-use stamp. Only the top of the tree is made public. To prove a stamp is real, you show it plus a few neighbouring branches so anyone can rebuild the path to the top.

sections.title: HSS: Trees of Trees
sections.content:
A single big tree makes key generation slow, because every LM-OTS public key must be generated first. The Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) uses a chain of L LMS trees. The root tree's public key is the HSS public key. Each tree signs the public key of the next one, and the bottom tree signs the actual message.

When the bottom tree runs out of leaves, the signer generates a fresh tree and has the tree above it sign the new tree's public key, recursing upward if that tree is used up too. If the top tree is exhausted, the HSS key pair MUST NOT generate any more signatures. The signer MUST NOT change the parameter set used at a given level.

The cost is a bigger signature and slower verification. The RFC's measurements, taken with W=8 on a 3.3 GHz Xeon, show the trade: a single tree of height 25 takes 1.5 hours to generate a key and has a 1936-byte signature, while a 25/15 two-level set generates a key in the same time with a 3652-byte signature and a key lifetime of 34 years at 1000 signatures per second. The RFC stresses that these timings are only a guideline.
sections.eli5: Instead of building one giant book of stamps up front, you build a small book now. When it runs out, a bigger boss book vouches for a fresh small one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The hash function H MUST have second preimage resistance: given one message, it must be infeasible to find a different message with the same hash. LMS is provably secure in the random oracle model, and the RFC quotes an analysis result saying that for no more than 2^64 randomly chosen LMS private keys and at most 2^120 hash compression computations, the chance of any single forgery is less than 2^-129.

Verifiers MUST check every typecode, and a signature with an unknown type or one that does not match the public key type MUST return INVALID. Lengths are implied by the typecode, so an object of the wrong length is invalid.

The biggest practical issue is statefulness. The updated key must really reach physical storage, which may require special steps such as the POSIX O_SYNC flag and flushing any on-drive cache. For hierarchical keys, implementations SHOULD keep the second-level private key in RAM only and regenerate it on restart, so that crashes and power failures are automatically accommodated.
sections.eli5: The main safety rule is to write down that a stamp has been used before you hand out the signed page. If the lights go out in between, you might use the same stamp twice and a cheat could take advantage.
